subject: Samhällskunskap
title: Personal finance
sourceSummary: Your own finances — income and expenses, how to make a budget, saving and loans, the difference between needs and wants, and how advertising influences you and what rights you have as a consumer.

questions.opener: Think about which way the money moves — in or out?
choices: Money that comes in to you, for example wages or an allowance
Money you have left in your account at the end of the month
Money you have put into a savings account
Money you pay out for something, for example a bus pass or a phone plan
questions.explanation: An expense is money that goes out, for example on food, the bus or a phone. Money that comes in is instead called income — and what's left once the expenses are paid is a surplus that can be saved.

questions.opener: A budget is made in advance, not afterwards.
choices: A plan for the income and expenses you expect over a certain period
A list of everything you already bought last year
A loan you take out from the bank
Another word for your entire savings account
questions.explanation: A budget is a plan looking forward: you list your expected income and expenses, for example for a month, and see whether the money will stretch far enough. A list of purchases already made is instead a follow-up on how things actually turned out.

questions.prompt: You get 500 kr a month in allowance and have expenses of 380 kr during the month. How much can you save?
choices: 880 kr
180 kr
120 kr
0 kr
questions.explanation: 500 kr − 380 kr = 120 kr, which is the surplus you can save. You get 880 kr if you mistakenly add income and expenses together instead of subtracting.

questions.prompt: What is interest on a loan?
questions.opener: It's the price of a service — being allowed to borrow someone else's money.
choices: A discount you get when you borrow money
The cost of borrowing money — extra money you pay on top of the loan amount itself
A fee the bank pays you when you take out a loan
Another word for how many months the loan lasts
questions.explanation: Interest is what it costs to borrow: you pay back the loan amount plus an extra percentage. On a savings account it works the other way round — then it's the bank that pays you interest for saving.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a need rather than a want?
questions.opener: A need is something you can't manage without.
choices: A new game for the console
Branded clothes from a particular shop
A more expensive phone case
Food and somewhere to live
questions.explanation: Needs are things you must have to get by, such as food, housing and clothes that keep you warm. A new game or branded clothes are wants — things that are nice to have but that you can manage without, and that's usually where you can save money.

questions.prompt: What does the right of withdrawal mean when you shop online?
questions.opener: The rule gives you a certain amount of time to change your mind after the item arrives home.
choices: That you can never return anything you've ordered
That the shop can cancel your order whenever it likes
That you usually have 14 days to change your mind and return the item
That you can only exchange the item for another one at the same shop
questions.explanation: For purchases online or by phone, you usually have a legal right of withdrawal of 14 days counted from when you received the item, and you don't need to give a reason. Certain goods are exempt, for example custom-made products and downloaded digital media — but the right of withdrawal is not the same thing as the voluntary exchange policy that shops can offer in a physical store.

questions.prompt: You get 400 kr a month in allowance and earn 300 kr from a side job. Your expenses are 99 kr for your phone, 150 kr for a bus pass, and 200 kr for coffee and treats and entertainment. How much can you save per month, and how many months does it take to save up for headphones costing 1,500 kr?
questions.opener: Add up the income first, then the expenses, and compare.
questions.answer: You can save 251 kr per month, and it takes 6 months to save up for the headphones.
steps: Add up the income: 400 kr + 300 kr = 700 kr.
Add up the expenses: 99 kr + 150 kr + 200 kr = 449 kr.
Work out the surplus: 700 kr − 449 kr = 251 kr that you can save each month.
Divide the goal by the savings amount: 1,500 / 251 ≈ 5.98 months.
Since you only save once a month, you have to round up: it takes 6 months.

questions.prompt: Summarise the basics of personal finance and consumer rights.
questions.opener: Go through income and expenses, budget, saving and loans, needs and wants, and your rights.
questions.answer: Income: money in — wages, allowance, study grants · Expense: money out — food, bus, phone, subscriptions · Surplus: income minus expenses, what you can save · Deficit: expenses are greater than income, then something has to change · Budget: a plan for coming income and expenses, usually per month · Fixed expenses: the same every month, e.g. subscriptions and a bus pass · Variable expenses: they vary, e.g. entertainment and clothes · Saving: money you set aside, the bank pays you interest · Loans: money you're allowed to borrow and pay back, you pay the bank interest — expensive payday loans and instalment plans can quickly become a debt trap · Needs: what you can't manage without (food, housing, clothes) · Wants: what you can manage without but would like to have · Advertising: wants to get you to buy, often through emotions, influencers and time pressure — hidden advertising must be labelled as an ad · Consumer rights: 14 days' right of withdrawal for online purchases, a 3-year right to complain if an item is faulty, always keep the receipt · Help and advice: the Hallå konsument consumer advice service and the municipality's consumer advisers.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between gross pay and net pay?
questions.opener: Think about what gets deducted before the money reaches your account.
choices: Gross pay is the wage before tax is deducted, net pay is what you get after tax
They are exactly the same thing
Net pay is always higher than gross pay
Gross pay is only paid to companies
questions.explanation: Gross pay is the full wage before tax is deducted, while net pay is what is actually paid out to you after tax has been subtracted. Net pay is therefore always lower than or equal to gross pay, never higher.

questions.prompt: What is the advantage of saving money in a savings account compared to keeping it as cash at home?
questions.opener: Think about both safety and whether the money can grow in value.
choices: The money grows through interest and is safer against things like theft or fire
There is no advantage at all
Cash at home always earns more interest
The bank automatically takes the money if you save it there
questions.explanation: Money in a savings account is protected by the bank against things like theft and fire, and the bank also pays interest so the money grows a little over time. Cash at home earns no interest at all and is more exposed if something were to happen at home.

questions.prompt: A student has money left over after buying food and the bus pass needed to get to school. Which of the following is an example of a want the student could choose to spend the money on?
questions.opener: A want is nice to have but not something you must have to get by.
choices: More textbooks required for the course
A cinema ticket just for fun
More food if it's actually needed
A new bus pass if the old one has expired and is needed for the trip to school
questions.explanation: A cinema ticket is a want — something fun to treat yourself to but that you can manage without. Textbooks required for the course, food you actually need, and a bus pass to get to school are instead needs, since they are necessary.

questions.prompt: What is the right to complain (reklamationsrätt)?
questions.opener: Unlike the right of withdrawal, the item must actually be faulty, not just something you changed your mind about.
choices: The right to complain, within a certain time, normally 3 years, about an item that was already faulty at the time of purchase
The right to always change your mind about an item for no reason
The right to never have to pay for an item
The right to complain about an item after an unlimited time with no receipt
questions.explanation: The right to complain gives you the right to complain about an item that is faulty, normally within three years of purchase, and the seller should then repair it, exchange it, or refund your money. This differs from the right of withdrawal, which applies even if the item is completely fault-free but you've simply changed your mind.

questions.prompt: How does advertising often influence consumers?
questions.opener: Think about what means advertising usually uses to make you want to buy something.
choices: Advertising is always completely objective fact
Advertising wants to stir up emotions and create wants, often by linking the item to status or happiness
Advertising is never allowed to be shown to children in Sweden
Advertising has no influence at all on purchasing decisions
questions.explanation: Advertising often tries to influence emotions rather than just provide factual information, for example by linking a product to status, belonging or happiness. That makes it important to be critical of advertising too, and to separate what you actually need from what the advertising makes you want.

questions.prompt: Your fixed expenses are 800 kr per month and your variable expenses usually range between 200 and 400 kr. What is most important to think about when planning your budget?
questions.opener: Think about what happens if a month turns out more expensive than usual.
choices: You only need to think about the fixed expenses
You should plan for the highest possible level of the variable expenses so the money is enough even in a more expensive month
You can ignore the variable expenses completely
You should always assume the variable expenses will be 0 kr
questions.explanation: By budgeting for the higher level of variable expenses, you make sure the money is enough even in months when the variable costs turn out higher. If you only account for the fixed expenses or assume the variable ones will be zero, you risk the money not being enough.

questions.prompt: What risks can payday loans involve?
questions.opener: Think about how the interest rate on a payday loan usually compares to other loans.
choices: Payday loans often have high interest and can quickly lead to a debt trap if you can't pay back on time
Payday loans are always interest-free
Payday loans are the cheapest form of loan
Payday loans involve no risks at all
questions.explanation: Payday loans often have a very high interest rate compared to ordinary bank loans, and if you can't pay back on time, the debt grows quickly through interest and fees. This means payday loans and similar instalment plans can easily lead to a debt trap that's hard to get out of.
